case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title VII requires a heightened prima facie showing for “majority-group” plaintiffs—specifically, that they prove “background circumstances” suggesting the employer is the unusual one that discriminates against the majority—in addition to the ordinary McDonnell Douglas elements.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, primarily 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a) (prohibiting employment discrimination “because of” race, color, religion, sex, or national origin).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Ames argues Title VII’s text protects “any individual” and does not allow courts to impose an extra, judge-made “background circumstances” hurdle on plaintiffs who are in a majority group. She contends the Sixth Circuit’s rule improperly creates unequal evidentiary burdens based on the plaintiff’s protected-class status (e.g., white/straight/male), conflicts with Title VII’s neutrality and this Court’s approach to Title VII proof frameworks, and should be rejected so majority-group plaintiffs proceed under the same prima facie standard as everyone else.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Ohio Department of Youth Services defends the Sixth Circuit’s requirement (and/or argues affirmance is appropriate regardless) on the theory that in “reverse discrimination” cases the usual inference of discrimination from basic prima facie facts is less warranted, so an added “background circumstances” showing is needed to justify an inference that the employer discriminated against the majority. It also argues the case is a poor vehicle: Ames allegedly did not squarely attack the legal validity of the Sixth Circuit test below (instead arguing she satisfied it), and in any event her demotion claim fails on independent grounds (e.g., lack of pretext), making the disputed prima facie element non-dispositive.
key_precedents: State v. Sum, 511 P.3d 92 (Wash. 2022) (referenced in an amicus brief for race-conscious standards in another context)

John Roberts.reasoning: Respondent’s best point remains pragmatic: because McDonnell Douglas is judge-made, courts can tailor the prima facie case to screen weaker “reverse discrimination” suits at summary judgment. But as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett emphasize via McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail, Title VII protects individuals “upon the same standards,” and a categorical “background circumstances” surcharge keyed to majority status is a status-based asymmetry that lacks textual footing in “any individual” and invites uneven administration. Justice Thomas’s reminder from Aikens/Hicks that McDonnell Douglas must not displace the statute’s ultimate “because of” inquiry reinforces that adding an extra prima facie element risks hardening an evidentiary tool into a nontextual barrier. A minimalist resolution is to hold only that Title VII and our precedents do not permit a categorical background-circumstances requirement, leaving ordinary McDonnell Douglas application and pretext analysis to the lower courts on remand.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Respondent’s strongest point—echoed by several colleagues as a pragmatic screening rationale—is that McDonnell Douglas may be tailored to reflect the asserted rarity of “reverse” discrimination and to weed out weak claims at summary judgment. But as Justice Gorsuch explains, that move makes the plaintiff’s protected trait itself do legal work in accessing the inference, which is irreconcilable with Title VII’s text protecting “any individual” and with separation-of-powers limits on judge-made add-ons. Justice Barrett’s invocation of McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail confirms that our precedents require the same standards for majority and minority plaintiffs, so the Sixth Circuit’s categorical “background circumstances” surcharge cannot be defended as mere flexibility within McDonnell Douglas. The ordinary framework already allows employers to prevail through legitimate reasons and pretext analysis, so the extra element is neither textually grounded nor necessary to preserve the statute’s “because of” inquiry.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the pragmatic one—raised by Justice Roberts and others—that McDonnell Douglas is judge-made and can be tailored to screen weak “reverse discrimination” suits; but that kind of tailoring cannot be keyed to the plaintiff’s majority status when Title VII protects “any individual” and our precedents reject different standards based on group membership. Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail is especially damaging to the Sixth Circuit rule because it squarely rejects asymmetric “standards” for majority plaintiffs, and the “background circumstances” requirement is precisely that. The respondent’s policy concern is adequately addressed by the existing McDonnell Douglas stages (legitimate reason and pretext) and by summary judgment’s evidentiary demands, without inserting a nontextual, hard-to-administer threshold that risks displacing the statute’s ultimate “because of” inquiry as Justice Thomas warns. On a textualist approach attentive to administrability and consequences, the Sixth Circuit’s categorical surcharge is not a permissible refinement but an unjustified distortion.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest argument—efficiency and screening of weak “reverse discrimination” suits—does not justify a plaintiff-status-based prima facie surcharge, because Title VII’s text protects “any individual” and our doctrine treats McDonnell Douglas as an evidentiary aid, not a courthouse-door barrier. Justice Barrett’s reliance on McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail is especially persuasive: it squarely rejects different “standards” for majority versus minority plaintiffs, making the Sixth Circuit’s “background circumstances” requirement hard to defend without rewriting the statute. Justice Kagan’s workability point reinforces my pragmatic concern that an asymmetric threshold will predictably foreclose claims—often at summary judgment—without testing the real-world context that can reveal discrimination. Employers remain protected by the legitimate-reason and pretext stages and the plaintiff’s ultimate burden of proving “because of,” so the added hurdle is both unnecessary and unfair in operation.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Respondent’s best point remains pragmatic—that a “background circumstances” requirement prevents weak reverse-discrimination suits from reaching juries—but that is a policy calibration that cannot be implemented by sorting plaintiffs by protected status when Title VII protects “any individual.” Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on the statute’s neutral text, together with Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail’s instruction that majority plaintiffs proceed “upon the same standards,” confirms the asymmetrical surcharge lacks a textual or precedential anchor. The concerns about workability and screening can be handled within the ordinary McDonnell Douglas structure—especially at the legitimate-reason and pretext stages—consistent with Aikens/Furnco’s warning against rigid, mechanized prima facie hurdles. Nothing in Burdine, Hicks, or Reeves authorizes hardening the prima facie case into a plaintiff-status-based extra element, so I would reverse.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The strongest likely argument for respondent is that McDonnell Douglas is a judge-made screening device and courts may sensibly calibrate its prima facie showing to account for the (claimed) lower baseline probability of “reverse” discrimination; but that is policy reasoning untethered to Title VII’s neutral command protecting “any individual” and it improperly makes the plaintiff’s protected trait do work in determining access to an inference. Justice Barrett’s reliance on McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail—that majority plaintiffs proceed “upon the same standards”—reinforces that our precedents reject asymmetrical standards keyed to group status, and it undercuts any attempt to defend a categorical “background circumstances” add-on as consistent with our law. Justice Sotomayor’s point that McDonnell Douglas was never meant to be rigid confirms the problem: the Sixth Circuit’s rule hardens a flexible evidentiary framework into an extra element for one set of plaintiffs. Applying the statute as written and keeping McDonnell Douglas uniform respects separation of powers and leaves any asymmetric thresholds to Congress, not courts.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Respondent’s best point remains pragmatic—that a “background circumstances” screen might more efficiently weed out weak reverse-discrimination suits—but that policy premise cannot justify a plaintiff-status-based prima facie surcharge absent textual or precedential footing. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett correctly anchor the analysis in Title VII’s protection of “any individual” and McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail’s instruction that majority and minority plaintiffs proceed “upon the same standards,” which squarely undermines a categorical asymmetric requirement. Justice Thomas’s emphasis on Aikens/Furnco reinforces my institutional concern: hardening McDonnell Douglas into group-contingent gatekeeping risks displacing the statute’s ultimate “because of” inquiry and invites uneven administration. Weak claims can be resolved at the legitimate-reason and pretext stages, preserving uniformity and administrability without rewriting the framework based on the plaintiff’s protected status.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument remains that McDonnell Douglas is a judge-made inference framework that can be tailored to reflect the purported rarity of majority-group discrimination, but that pragmatic premise cannot justify a categorical, plaintiff-status-based extra element absent any grounding in Title VII’s text protecting “any individual.” Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh persuasively link the point to McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail, which rejects different “standards” for majority and minority plaintiffs, undermining the Sixth Circuit’s “background circumstances” surcharge. Justice Thomas’s reminder from Aikens and Hicks that McDonnell Douglas must not displace the statute’s ultimate “because of” inquiry reinforces that hardening the prima facie case into a group-contingent threshold is methodologically inconsistent with our precedents. Employers’ efficiency concerns can be handled through the ordinary legitimate-reason and pretext analysis rather than by rewriting prima facie elements keyed to protected status.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—echoed by the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh—is pragmatic: McDonnell Douglas is judge-made, so courts can calibrate the prima facie inference to filter weak “reverse discrimination” claims at summary judgment. But as Justice Barrett stresses via McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail, Title VII plaintiffs proceed “upon the same standards,” and a categorical “background circumstances” surcharge tied to majority status conflicts with that neutrality and with Title VII’s “any individual” text. Justice Sotomayor’s reminder that McDonnell Douglas was never meant to be rigid reinforces that the proper place to test evidentiary strength is the legitimate-reason and pretext stages, not by adding a plaintiff-status-based gatekeeping element. Aikens/Furnco and related cases caution against mechanizing the framework in a way that displaces the statute’s ultimate “because of” inquiry, so I remain persuaded reversal is required.

John Roberts.reasoning: Title VII makes it unlawful for an employer to discriminate against “any individual” because of race, sex, and other protected traits, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a), and our cases emphasize that the statute’s focus is on individuals rather than group-based rules. The McDonnell Douglas framework is a flexible, judge-made evidentiary tool to permit an inference of discrimination from circumstantial proof, not a license to impose a plaintiff-status-based extra hurdle; nothing in McDonnell Douglas conditions the prima facie case on minority status. We have also made clear that Title VII prohibits “discriminatory preference for any group, minority or majority,” Griggs v. Duke Power Co., 401 U.S. 424, 431 (1971), and applied Title VII protections evenhandedly to white plaintiffs as well, McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transp. Co., 427 U.S. 273, 279–80 (1976). A narrow disposition rejecting a categorical “background circumstances” requirement best adheres to the statute’s text, preserves the uniformity and administrability of McDonnell Douglas, and protects institutional legitimacy by avoiding judge-made distinctions that turn on the plaintiff’s protected status.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Title VII’s text makes it unlawful for an employer to discriminate against “any individual” “because of” race or sex, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and it contains no basis for imposing a special, heightened prima facie requirement on so-called “majority-group” plaintiffs. McDonnell Douglas established a flexible, judge-made ordering of proof for circumstantial-evidence cases, not a license for courts to add nontextual elements that vary by the plaintiff’s protected-class status. As St. Mary’s Honor Ctr. v. Hicks explains, the McDonnell Douglas framework cannot supplant the statute’s ultimate question—whether the employer acted because of a protected trait—so an extra “background circumstances” hurdle improperly displaces the statutory inquiry. Because the Sixth Circuit’s rule creates an asymmetrical evidentiary burden not found in the enacted text, I would reverse and require the ordinary McDonnell Douglas elements to apply equally to all plaintiffs.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Title VII’s operative text makes it unlawful to discriminate against “any individual” “because of such individual’s race, color, religion, sex, or national origin,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and it does not authorize a plaintiff-status-based, extra prima facie element for “majority-group” plaintiffs. McDonnell Douglas established a pragmatic, burden-shifting evidentiary framework to smoke out discriminatory intent, not a license for courts to ratchet up threshold showings depending on which group the plaintiff is in. The “background circumstances” requirement risks creating unequal procedural burdens untethered to the statutory language and would invite inconsistent, hard-to-administer line-drawing with questionable practical benefits at summary judgment. While the respondent’s vehicle arguments may bear on disposition on remand (e.g., pretext), the Sixth Circuit’s added prima facie hurdle itself is inconsistent with the statute and this Court’s uniform application of McDonnell Douglas.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title VII’s text makes it unlawful for an employer to discriminate against “any individual” because of race, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a), and this Court has recognized that the statute protects majority and minority employees alike. The McDonnell Douglas framework is a pragmatic evidentiary tool meant to be flexible across employment contexts, but not to impose different prima facie burdens based on the plaintiff’s race; as Aikens cautioned, it was “never intended to be rigid, mechanized, or ritualistic.” Requiring “background circumstances” for majority-group plaintiffs improperly adds a judge-made, unequal threshold that can shut the courthouse door without advancing Title VII’s core inquiry—whether the challenged action was “because of” a protected trait—contrary to the inference-focused approach described in Furnco and Burdine. Equal access to justice and fair evidentiary rules counsel applying the ordinary McDonnell Douglas prima facie standard to all plaintiffs.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Title VII’s text makes it unlawful for an employer to discriminate against “any individual” because of protected traits, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and nothing in that language supports a plaintiff-status-based evidentiary surcharge for “majority-group” plaintiffs. McDonnell Douglas established a pragmatic, workability-oriented burden-shifting framework to help surface discriminatory intent, not a license to ratchet the prima facie case up or down depending on whether the plaintiff is in a numerical majority. Consistent with Burdine and Reeves, the prima facie showing is meant to eliminate common nondiscriminatory explanations and then test the employer’s reason for pretext; a “background circumstances” requirement improperly hardens a flexible inference into an extra element that can foreclose otherwise viable claims at summary judgment. A uniform prima facie standard better fits statutory coherence and Title VII’s neutrality while preserving the employer’s ability to win on legitimate reasons and the plaintiff’s ultimate burden to prove discriminatory purpose.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Title VII makes it unlawful for an employer to discriminate against “any individual” “because of such individual’s race, color, religion, sex, or national origin,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and nothing in that text authorizes courts to impose a higher prima facie burden on plaintiffs based solely on their majority-group status. The judge-made “background circumstances” requirement sorts litigants by the very protected characteristics the statute treats neutrally, contrary to our instruction that Title VII focuses on individuals rather than groups. McDonnell Douglas provides an evidentiary framework for proving discriminatory intent, but it does not license adding an extra element for one set of plaintiffs; indeed it echoes Griggs’s statement that discriminatory preference for “any group, minority or majority,” is what Congress proscribed. Consistent with separation-of-powers principles, we should apply the statute as written and leave such policy-driven asymmetries to Congress, not the courts.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Title VII’s text makes it unlawful to discriminate against “any individual” because of race or sex, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and this Court has held that protection applies equally to majority and minority employees. In McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transp. Co., 427 U.S. 273, 279 (1976), we rejected the notion that Title VII’s coverage turns on whether the plaintiff is in a “minority or majority” group, which cuts strongly against a judge-made, class-specific “background circumstances” hurdle. McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973), established a flexible evidentiary framework for circumstantial proof, and our subsequent cases emphasize its workability and limited role—not as a license for courts to impose asymmetric prima facie burdens untethered to statutory text. As an institutional matter, a uniform prima facie standard better aligns with precedent, avoids unnecessary doctrinal complexity, and preserves Title VII’s neutral, administrable rule of decision.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Title VII’s text makes it unlawful to discriminate against “any individual” because of race, sex, or other protected traits, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and nothing in that language authorizes a court-imposed, plaintiff-status-based “background circumstances” hurdle. This Court has already held that Title VII protects majority-group plaintiffs “upon the same standards” as minority-group plaintiffs. McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transp. Co., 427 U.S. 273, 280 (1976). The McDonnell Douglas framework is an evidentiary method to “evaluate the evidence,” not a license to vary prima facie elements by group membership, Furnco Constr. Corp. v. Waters, 438 U.S. 567, 577 (1978), and adopting a heightened showing risks contradicting the statute’s individual-focused command. Precedent and methodological consistency thus favor applying the ordinary McDonnell Douglas prima facie requirements without an additional majority-plaintiff element.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title VII’s text makes it unlawful for an employer to discriminate against “any individual” because of race, sex, or other protected traits, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and that neutral command does not authorize courts to impose an extra, plaintiff-status-based prima facie hurdle on “majority-group” plaintiffs. McDonnell Douglas provides a flexible evidentiary framework for inferring discriminatory intent, but it does not endorse adding a “background circumstances” requirement that turns on the plaintiff’s group membership; indeed it echoes Griggs’s instruction that discriminatory preference for “any group, minority or majority” is what Congress proscribed. Creating different prima facie burdens based on whether a plaintiff is in a perceived majority undermines procedural fairness and risks skewing practical outcomes at summary judgment by screening out potentially meritorious claims on a judge-made threshold unrelated to the employer’s treatment of the individual. Consistent with Bostock’s emphasis that Title VII focuses on individuals rather than groups, the Court should reject the heightened requirement and apply the ordinary McDonnell Douglas elements uniformly.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a Title VII plaintiff who is a member of a majority group must satisfy a heightened prima facie burden—often phrased as showing “background circumstances” suggesting the employer is the unusual one that discriminates against the majority—before the case can proceed under the McDonnell Douglas framework.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq. (especially § 2000e-2(a) prohibiting discrimination in employment “because of” race/sex and related protected traits).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Ames argues that Title VII’s text protects “any individual” from discrimination because of protected characteristics, so courts cannot impose an extra, judge-made prima facie element on “majority-group” plaintiffs. Requiring “background circumstances” (i.e., special evidence that the employer is the unusual employer who discriminates against the majority) creates an asymmetric, higher pleading/proof gateway that conflicts with Title VII’s neutral language and the ordinary McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting structure. The proper rule is that majority- and minority-group plaintiffs should face the same prima facie showing and have their claims evaluated under the same evidentiary framework without race- or sex-based add-ons.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Ohio Department of Youth Services defends the Sixth Circuit’s approach (or at least the judgment below), contending that in so-called “reverse discrimination” cases the prima facie case can properly require some “background circumstances” indicating a plausible inference of discrimination against a majority-group member. The respondent also emphasizes case-specific reasons the claim fails on the merits (including the lower court’s conclusions regarding lack of pretext for challenged actions) and argues that the case may be a poor vehicle to resolve the doctrinal question because Ames did not squarely attack the Sixth Circuit’s “background circumstances” requirement in the lower courts and because other dispositive merits holdings limit what relief she could obtain even if the prima facie standard were changed.

Justice Kagan’s reminder that Burdine describes the prima facie showing as “not onerous,” together with Hicks/Reeves, reinforces that McDonnell Douglas is a flexible evidentiary ordering and cannot be converted into asymmetric gatekeeping. Justice Alito’s reliance on McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail is particularly salient: it confirms symmetrical statutory coverage, making it difficult to square a heightened threshold for majority plaintiffs with our precedents and institutional legitimacy concerns about judge-made variability across circuits. A narrow holding—rejecting any categorical “background circumstances” requirement while leaving ordinary summary-judgment scrutiny and the pretext inquiry to do their work—best preserves precedent and keeps the focus on the statutory causation question.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest respondent-side contention would be that a “background circumstances” requirement is a sensible, experience-based screening device because discrimination against majority groups is supposedly less likely; but that policy premise cannot justify adding an atextual element to § 2000e-2(a)(1), which protects “any individual” and turns solely on whether an action was taken “because of” race or sex. Justice Alito’s reliance on McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail confirms the statute applies symmetrically, and Justice Gorsuch correctly notes that varying the prima facie case by group status raises separation-of-powers concerns by rewriting the evidentiary gateway beyond what Congress enacted. McDonnell Douglas is an evidentiary ordering that may assist factfinding, but under Hicks and Reeves it cannot displace the statutory question; any concern about weak cases is handled at summary judgment and the pretext stage without imposing categorical, status-based hurdles. Nothing in the text or our precedents authorizes courts to require majority plaintiffs to prove extra “background circumstances” before they may invoke the same inferential framework available to everyone else.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains pragmatic: majority-group discrimination may be less common, so a “background circumstances” screen might conserve judicial and employer resources. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas stress, Title VII’s text protects “any individual,” and neither § 2000e-2(a)(1) nor McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail supports grafting a plaintiff-status-dependent element onto the prima facie case. Justice Kagan’s workability point is persuasive under our precedents—Burdine’s “not onerous” prima facie showing and Hicks/Reeves’ focus on the ultimate “because of” question—because weak cases can be resolved at summary judgment and at the pretext stage without rewriting McDonnell Douglas into an asymmetric, judge-made gatekeeping rule. On a textualist approach attentive to practical consequences, the uniform prima facie standard better preserves statutory symmetry while still allowing rigorous merits screening later in the framework.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that “background circumstances” pragmatically screens out speculative reverse-discrimination claims—does not justify a categorical, group-status-dependent barrier at the prima facie stage when ordinary summary-judgment standards, the employer’s legitimate-reason step, and the pretext inquiry already police weak cases without denying access to the inferential framework. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on Title VII’s text protecting “any individual” underscores that an asymmetric prima facie gateway lacks statutory footing and risks uneven access to justice. Justice Kagan’s reminder (via Burdine) that the prima facie showing is “not onerous” is especially important in practice: adding an extra element turns an inference mechanism into a heightened merits hurdle that will disproportionately shut out plaintiffs who lack direct evidence. Justice Alito’s reliance on McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail further confirms Title VII’s symmetrical protection, making it particularly problematic—both doctrinally and in real-world effect—to condition the prima facie case on majority status.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains pragmatic: “background circumstances” supposedly calibrates McDonnell Douglas because majority-group discrimination is less common, so the usual prima facie inference is weaker. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, McDonnell Douglas is a flexible, judge-made order-of-proof device whose step-one showing is “not onerous,” and converting it into a plaintiff-status-dependent gatekeeping rule creates an asymmetry that the text (“any individual”) does not support and that undermines coherent, uniform administration. Justice Alito’s reliance on McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail strengthens the symmetry point: if Title VII’s substantive coverage is evenhanded, the prima facie framework should not impose extra elements on one set of plaintiffs. The screening concern can be handled where it belongs—at the legitimate-reason and pretext stages under Hicks/Reeves and ordinary summary-judgment scrutiny—without distorting step one.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains pragmatic—that “background circumstances” is needed to prevent weak reverse-discrimination claims from generating an inference too easily—but that is a policy judgment that cannot justify adding a status-based element nowhere found in Title VII’s text protecting “any individual.” Chief Justice Roberts is right that McDonnell Douglas is only a flexible order-of-proof device; converting it into an asymmetric gatekeeping rule conflicts with Burdine’s instruction that the prima facie showing is “not onerous” and with Hicks/Reeves warning against letting judge-made frameworks displace the statutory “because of” inquiry. Justice Alito’s citation to McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail underscores the symmetry Congress adopted and makes it especially difficult, as a matter of text and precedent, to defend a majority-only heightened threshold. Any workability concern is better handled at the legitimate-reason and pretext stages and through ordinary summary-judgment principles rather than rewriting the prima facie case.

Santa Fe Trail reinforces that Title VII’s protections are symmetrical, making it especially difficult to justify an asymmetric threshold at step one, particularly given Burdine’s admonition (noted by Justice Kagan) that the prima facie showing is “not onerous.” Any workability concerns can be handled through the employer’s legitimate-reason step, the plaintiff’s pretext showing under Hicks/Reeves, and ordinary summary-judgment scrutiny without rewriting the prima facie case by group status.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains pragmatic: “background circumstances” supposedly prevents weak reverse-discrimination claims from triggering an inference too easily, but that is not a procedurally fair reason to impose a status-based gateway that Title VII’s text does not contain. Santa Fe Trail further undercuts any attempt to make prima facie elements depend on whether the plaintiff is in a majority or minority group, because Title VII protects “any individual” on symmetrical terms. On a progressive-pragmatist view attentive to real-world access to adjudication, the added requirement risks prematurely terminating potentially meritorious claims without any corresponding statutory authorization.

McDonnell Douglas established a flexible, “modes and orders of proof” framework designed to permit an inference of discrimination from circumstantial evidence, not a license for courts to add extra judge-made elements that vary by the plaintiff’s group status. Hicks and Reeves), the “background circumstances” requirement risks distorting the merits and undermining uniformity and institutional legitimacy. Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Title VII’s text makes it unlawful for an employer to discriminate against “any individual” “because of” race or sex, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and that neutral language does not authorize a judge-made, heightened prima facie hurdle for majority-group plaintiffs. Hicks confirms, the ultimate question remains whether the employer acted “because of” a protected trait, and courts may not let a nontextual framework supplant the statute. Imposing a “background circumstances” requirement rewrites Title VII and departs from the equal application demanded by the statutory text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Title VII’s text makes it an unlawful employment practice to discriminate against “any individual” because of race or sex, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and this Court has confirmed that the provision protects majority and minority employees alike. McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transp. Co., 427 U.S. 273, 279 (1976). Because McDonnell Douglas is a judge-made evidentiary framework designed to “sharpen the inquiry” into discriminatory intent, 411 U.S. at 802–804, courts should not graft onto it a heightened, asymmetric “background circumstances” prerequisite that effectively rewrites the prima facie case based on the plaintiff’s group status. Whatever the practical attraction of screening weak claims, that concern is addressed at the pretext stage and by summary-judgment standards, not by imposing atextual, group-based gatekeeping inconsistent with § 2000e-2(a)(1).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title VII’s text forbids discrimination against “any individual” because of race or sex, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and nothing in that neutral language authorizes courts to impose a higher, judge-made gateway burden on majority-group plaintiffs. McDonnell Douglas provides a common, practical evidentiary framework for circumstantial cases, and Burdine emphasizes the prima facie showing is “not onerous”; a “background circumstances” requirement improperly converts that modest screening step into an asymmetric merits hurdle. As a matter of fairness and access to justice, especially for employees without direct evidence, the same prima facie structure should apply to all plaintiffs, with the ultimate question of intentional discrimination resolved through the ordinary burden-shifting and pretext inquiry rather than categorical, status-based add-ons.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Title VII makes it unlawful for an employer to discriminate against “any individual” because of race or sex, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and nothing in that text authorizes a higher gateway burden for majority-group plaintiffs. The McDonnell Douglas framework is a workability device meant to “raise an inference of discrimination” through a “not onerous” prima facie showing, Burdine, 450 U.S. at 253, and importing a “background circumstances” element creates an asymmetrical, judge-made hurdle that conflicts with the statute’s neutral coverage and complicates administration without improving the ultimate merits inquiry. If an employer has a legitimate explanation, it can be tested at the rebuttal and pretext stages rather than by redefining who gets the presumption in the first place. The better, more coherent rule is a single prima facie standard for all Title VII plaintiffs, with the case turning—as the statute requires—on whether this plaintiff was treated adversely “because of” a protected trait.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Title VII’s operative text makes it unlawful to discriminate against “any individual … because of such individual’s race … [or] sex,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and nothing in that language authorizes courts to impose a higher, judge-made prima facie gateway on majority-group plaintiffs. McDonnell Douglas established a trans-substantive evidentiary framework for proving discrimination by circumstantial evidence, not a license to vary the prima facie elements based on the plaintiff’s protected class membership. A “background circumstances” requirement effectively adds an atextual element and introduces asymmetry that risks substituting judicial policy judgments for Congress’s neutral command, raising separation-of-powers concerns. The proper course is to apply the same McDonnell Douglas prima facie showing to all Title VII plaintiffs and allow merits questions (including pretext) to be resolved at later stages under the ordinary framework.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Title VII’s text makes it unlawful to discriminate against “any individual” because of race or sex, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and nothing in that neutral language authorizes courts to impose a heightened, plaintiff-class-dependent prima facie burden on majority-group plaintiffs. McDonnell Douglas established a flexible, judge-made evidentiary framework to screen circumstantial-evidence cases, not a license to add extra elements based on the plaintiff’s protected status, and later cases emphasize focusing on whether the evidence permits an inference of discrimination rather than rigid gatekeeping. A “background circumstances” requirement is difficult to square with the Court’s instruction that the prima facie showing is not meant to be onerous and creates unnecessary asymmetry that undermines workability and uniform administration of Title VII. Consistent with precedent, history, and institutional legitimacy, the Court should apply the same McDonnell Douglas prima facie formulation to all plaintiffs and leave any different treatment to Congress, not judicial gloss.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Title VII’s core prohibition makes it unlawful to discriminate against “any individual” “because of such individual’s race … [or] sex,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and that text contains no carveout authorizing a heightened prima facie gateway for majority-group plaintiffs. The McDonnell Douglas framework is a judge-made evidentiary method designed to aid proof by circumstantial evidence, not to add claimant-specific elements that vary with the plaintiff’s protected characteristic. Requiring “background circumstances” effectively makes the prima facie showing turn on group prevalence rather than whether the adverse action occurred “because of” the individual’s protected trait, which is methodologically inconsistent with the statute’s neutral phrasing and this Court’s articulation of Title VII’s purpose “to assure equality of employment opportunities.” McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792, 800 (1973). Precedent can be respected by retaining McDonnell Douglas’s ordinary elements while rejecting an extra, asymmetrical requirement that lacks textual footing in § 2000e-2(a)(1).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title VII’s text makes it unlawful for an employer to discriminate against “any individual” “because of” a protected trait, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a), and nothing in that neutral language authorizes courts to impose a higher threshold burden on majority-group plaintiffs. Our cases describe McDonnell Douglas as a flexible evidentiary framework meant to “eliminate[] the most common nondiscriminatory reasons” for an employment action, not as a license to create asymmetric, status-based gatekeeping requirements; Furnco Construction Corp. v. Waters emphasizes that the framework was “never intended to be rigid, mechanized, or ritualistic.” Heightening the prima facie showing for one set of plaintiffs undermines procedural fairness and risks practical consequences of foreclosing potentially meritorious claims based on a judge-made rule untethered to the statute. The proper course is to apply the same McDonnell Douglas prima facie standard to all Title VII plaintiffs, leaving the ultimate merits question—whether a reasonable jury could find intentional discrimination—to be resolved without a “background circumstances” add-on.
